questions.statement: Notice: Bring your draft poster to Room 12 before Thursday lunch for printing. What must you do first?
questions.context: Your class is preparing a science exhibition and you read the notice board before acting.

options.text: Take the draft poster to Room 12 before Thursday lunch.
options.feedback: Correct! Taking the draft poster to Room 12 before Thursday lunch uses the place, the object and the deadline exactly as the notice states.

options.text: Send the final poster by email on Friday evening.
options.feedback: This option fails because sending the final poster by email on Friday evening changes the place, the version and the deadline stated in the notice.

options.text: Buy printing paper at the shop after school.
options.feedback: This option fails because buying printing paper at the shop after school ignores the required object, place and deadline and invents a new shopping task.

options.text: Wait in Room 12 until Thursday lunch without the poster.
options.feedback: This option fails because waiting in Room 12 until Thursday lunch without the poster keeps the place and time but drops the essential object to deliver.

questions.explanation: Integrated reading means scanning an announcement for who, where and when, then turning those facts into one correct action instead of guessing from a single word.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Message: My train arrives at six and I am vegetarian. Which reply uses both pieces of information correctly?
questions.context: Your exchange partner sends an email about arrival time and food needs before your meeting.

options.text: I will meet you at the station at six with a vegetarian dinner ready.
options.feedback: Correct! Meeting at the station at six with a vegetarian dinner ready correctly reuses both the arrival time and the vegetarian need from the message.

options.text: I will meet you at midnight with a meat stew ready.
options.feedback: This option fails because meeting at midnight with a meat stew ready changes the stated six o clock arrival and contradicts the vegetarian need completely.

options.text: I will ignore your train and cook only fish soup.
options.feedback: This option fails because ignoring the train and cooking only fish soup drops the arrival information and fish soup does not satisfy a vegetarian request.

options.text: I will meet you at six but serve only beef burgers.
options.feedback: This option fails because meeting at six but serving only beef burgers keeps the time right yet directly violates the vegetarian need with beef burgers.

questions.explanation: A good written reply proves you understood two separate facts from reading and you reuse both accurately, which is the core of reading into writing integration.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: You hear: I lost my blue jacket near the gym yesterday. Which spoken response shows you understood and helps next?
questions.context: You listen to a classmate describing a lost jacket and you must respond with helpful speech.

options.text: Did you say a blue jacket near the gym yesterday, so shall we look there together?
options.feedback: Correct! Asking about the blue jacket lost near the gym yesterday repeats the color, place and time and offers concrete help to look there.

options.text: Did you lose a red hat in the library, so shall we buy a new one?
options.feedback: This option fails because asking about a red hat lost in the library changes the color, object and place that the classmate actually described.

options.text: I had pasta for lunch today and the canteen was very crowded at noon.
options.feedback: This option fails because talking about your own lunch menu ignores the lost jacket completely and offers no listening based response at all.

options.text: I never go to the gym, so I cannot help you with anything today.
options.feedback: This option fails because saying you never go to the gym dismisses the location detail and refuses the cooperative speaking move the task needs.

questions.explanation: Listening into speaking means catching the key details of what you heard and reflecting them back in a helpful spoken turn instead of giving a generic answer.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Timetable: Chemistry moves to Lab 3 at three. Note: Bring your notebook to chemistry. What will you do?
questions.context: You read a timetable change and a teacher note together before planning your afternoon.

options.text: Go to Lab 3 at three with your notebook ready.
options.feedback: Correct! Going to Lab 3 at three with your notebook combines the new room and time from the timetable with the notebook order from the teacher note.

options.text: Go to Lab 1 at two with a novel to read.
options.feedback: This option fails because going to Lab 1 at two with a novel uses the old timetable data and replaces the notebook with an unrelated novel.

options.text: Stay home at three with your notebook ready.
options.feedback: This option fails because staying home at three with your notebook keeps the notebook idea but disobeys the timetable change to attend Lab 3.

options.text: Go to Lab 3 at three without bringing anything.
options.feedback: This option fails because going to Lab 3 at three without anything respects the new timetable but drops the teacher instruction to bring your notebook.

questions.explanation: Real multitask reading forces you to combine two short texts and keep only the conclusion that respects both, discarding options that use just one source.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Guide: Member Diaz, card 4421, returns books on 12 May. Fill the card with the correct details.
questions.context: You read a library guide while filling in your new membership card at the desk.

options.text: Diaz, card 4421, return date 12 May.
options.feedback: Correct! Writing Diaz, card 4421, return date 12 May copies the surname, card number and date exactly as the guide and example card show.

options.text: Garcia, card 4421, return date 12 May.
options.feedback: This option fails because writing Garcia, card 4421, return date 12 May keeps number and date but changes the surname from Diaz to Garcia.

options.text: Diaz, card 2214, return date 12 May.
options.feedback: This option fails because writing Diaz, card 2214, return date 12 May keeps name and date but copies the wrong card number 2214.

options.text: Diaz, card 4421, return date 20 June.
options.feedback: This option fails because writing Diaz, card 4421, return date 20 June keeps name and number but invents a June date instead of 12 May.

questions.explanation: Form filling from reading trains selective transfer, copying names, numbers and dates exactly as printed while ignoring decorative information around them.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Subtitles: Bees pollinate one third of our food crops. Which notebook line best summarizes the video for tomorrow?
questions.context: You watch a short video with subtitles and take notes for a class summary the next day.

options.text: The video explains that bees pollinate one third of our food.
options.feedback: Correct! The video explains that bees pollinate one third of our food correctly condenses the subtitle message into one clear grammatical summary sentence.

options.text: The video shows bees eating one third of our food.
options.feedback: This option fails because the video shows bees eating one third of our food changes the verb pollinate to eating and reverses the scientific meaning.

options.text: The video sells televisions to one third of bees.
options.feedback: This option fails because the video sells televisions to one third of bees invents televisions and selling, which never appeared in the subtitles at all.

options.text: Bees, food, third, video.
options.feedback: This option fails because bees, food, third, video lists content words without a verb or structure and therefore is not a usable summary sentence.

questions.explanation: Watching with subtitles plus note taking builds the habit of turning spoken and written input together into a short grammatical sentence that keeps the main fact.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Steps: research the topic, make slides, rehearse aloud, present to class. Which order completes the multitask correctly?
questions.context: Your group must order the steps for a class presentation that mixes reading and speaking tasks.

options.text: Research, then slides, then rehearse, then present.
options.feedback: Correct! Research, then slides, then rehearse, then present follows the only logical workflow where each step prepares the material needed for the next step.

options.text: Present, then research, then slides, then rehearse.
options.feedback: This option fails because present, then research, then slides, then rehearse puts delivery first when there is nothing researched or prepared to deliver.

options.text: Rehearse, then present, then research, then slides.
options.feedback: This option fails because rehearse, then present, then research, then slides rehearses an empty talk and researches only after the presentation is finished.

options.text: Slides, then present, then research, then rehearse.
options.feedback: This option fails because slides, then present, then research, then rehearse makes slides before research and presents before any rehearsal has happened.

questions.explanation: Sequencing a multitask project teaches logical workflow, research must come before slides and rehearsal must come before delivery, or the later steps have no content.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Paragraph 1 praises city bikes. Paragraph 2 lists safety rules. Which sentence best connects both paragraphs?
questions.context: You are joining two paragraphs of a blog post with a linking sentence about city bikes.

options.text: This habit is useful, but riders must learn the safety rules below.
options.feedback: Correct! This habit is useful, but riders must learn the safety rules below correctly bridges the benefit idea to the rules paragraph that follows next.

options.text: Bikes were invented a long time ago in history.
options.feedback: This option fails because bikes were invented a long time ago in history drops the benefit thread and jumps to history instead of the coming safety rules.

options.text: I like pizza and films on weekends.
options.feedback: This option fails because I like pizza and films on weekends abandons the bike topic entirely and connects to nothing in either surrounding paragraph.

options.text: The rules are boring and nobody should read them.
options.feedback: This option fails because the rules are boring and nobody should read them contradicts the purpose of the second paragraph and breaks the forward link.

questions.explanation: Cohesive linking across paragraphs requires a bridge sentence that picks up the bike idea from paragraph one and points forward to safety rules in paragraph two.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Source: The school trip visited the river park. Summary: The trip visited the river park and the museum. What is the error?
questions.context: You compare a source text with a classmate summary to find the integration mistake.

options.text: The summary adds a museum never mentioned in the source.
options.feedback: Correct! Pointing out that the summary adds a museum never mentioned shows you compared every detail to the source and caught the invented integration error.

options.text: The summary is perfect and needs no change.
options.feedback: This option fails because saying the summary is perfect and needs no change misses the invented museum detail and shows no source comparison at all.

options.text: The summary has bad handwriting and spelling errors.
options.feedback: This option fails because complaining about handwriting and spelling focuses on appearance while ignoring the factual museum error in the content itself.

options.text: The source mentions a museum, so the summary is right.
options.feedback: This option fails because claiming the source mentions a museum defends the mistake and proves the comparison with the real source was not done.

questions.explanation: Checking a summary against its source trains critical reading, you must spot added, missing or twisted facts rather than trusting a fluent but faulty retelling.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Review: A small clean quiet hotel near the beach. Which sentence paraphrases it accurately for your travel diary?
questions.context: You read a hotel review and choose the paraphrase that keeps both meaning and grammar correct.

options.text: The small hotel near the beach was clean and quiet.
options.feedback: Correct! The small hotel near the beach was clean and quiet keeps small, beach location and positive evaluation with correct grammar throughout the sentence.

options.text: The huge hotel in the mountains was dirty and noisy.
options.feedback: This option fails because the huge hotel in the mountains was dirty and noisy changes size, location and evaluation, reversing almost every detail of the review.

options.text: The small hotel near the beach was dirty and noisy.
options.feedback: This option fails because the small hotel near the beach was dirty and noisy keeps size and place but flips clean and quiet into a negative judgment.

options.text: Hotel beach small clean quiet.
options.feedback: This option fails because hotel beach small clean quiet removes verbs and articles so the grammar collapses even though the content words look similar.

questions.explanation: Paraphrasing under test conditions means preserving tense, place and evaluation together, a single changed adjective or verb can flip praise into complaint.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Dialogue: Ana and Pablo will watch a film on Saturday. Which follow up question keeps the conversation going?
questions.context: After reading a dialogue about weekend plans you must ask a useful follow up question.

options.text: Shall we bring tickets for the Saturday film with Ana?
options.feedback: Correct! Asking if you should bring tickets for the Saturday film with Ana reuses the plan details and moves the joint decision forward naturally.

options.text: What did Ana eat for breakfast last year?
options.feedback: This option fails because asking what Ana ate for breakfast last year drops the weekend plan and jumps to an unrelated past meal.

options.text: Can fish ride bicycles in winter?
options.feedback: This option fails because asking whether fish can ride bicycles ignores Ana, Saturday and the film and breaks all links to the dialogue.

options.text: I hate cinemas and I will stay home.
options.feedback: This option fails because stating you hate cinemas and will stay home shuts down the joint plan instead of asking a cooperative follow up question.

questions.explanation: A strong follow up question proves integrated listening, it reuses names, times and intentions from the dialogue and pushes the joint plan one step forward.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Chart: showers 45 percent, garden 25 percent, drinking 5 percent. Article: cut shower time. Which conclusion uses both sources?
questions.context: You combine a bar chart on water use with a short article before drawing a conclusion.

options.text: Showers use the most water, so shorter showers save most.
options.feedback: Correct! Showers use the most water so shorter showers save most correctly reads the tallest bar and links it to the article advice about shower time.

options.text: Garden watering uses the most water of all uses.
options.feedback: This option fails because garden watering uses the most water misreads the chart since the shower bar is clearly taller than the garden bar.

options.text: Drinking water uses the most water of all uses.
options.feedback: This option fails because drinking water uses the most water confuses the smallest bar with the largest and ignores the article focus on showers.

options.text: Charts are useless and articles always lie.
options.feedback: This option fails because charts are useless and articles lie refuses to integrate either source and offers no evidence based conclusion at all.

questions.explanation: Chart plus text synthesis is a classic integrated skill, the correct conclusion must agree with the numbers in the graphic and the causes named in the article.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Task: write a formal email to your teacher asking about the project deadline. Which option fits best?
questions.context: You must reply to a teacher request and choose the register that fits a formal email.

options.text: Dear Mrs Lopez, could you please confirm the deadline?
options.feedback: Correct! Dear Mrs Lopez, could you please confirm the deadline uses a formal greeting, polite modal and full forms suited to a teacher email.

options.text: Hey Lopez, gimme the deadline now!
options.feedback: This option fails because Hey Lopez, gimme the deadline now uses a rude greeting plus slang gimme, which is wrong for a formal teacher email.

options.text: Yo teacher, what is up with homework?
options.feedback: This option fails because Yo teacher, what is up with homework uses street greeting and vague wording that ignores formal email conventions completely.

options.text: An emoji with no words.
options.feedback: This option fails because sending only an emoji with no words provides no greeting, request or polite structure needed for a formal written message.

questions.explanation: Register control is part of integrated writing, you read who will receive the message and then select formal openers, polite modals and full forms accordingly.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Report 1: Forty volunteers joined. Report 2: Three tons were collected. Which summary best integrates both reports?
questions.context: You read two river cleanup reports and judge which student summary integrates both texts well.

options.text: Forty volunteers joined and three tons were collected.
options.feedback: Correct! Praising the summary that names forty volunteers and three tons collected rewards coverage of both reports with exact numbers and no invented facts.

options.text: Forty volunteers joined the river event.
options.feedback: This option fails because praising the summary that mentions only volunteers rewards partial coverage and ignores the three tons fact from the second report.

options.text: Three tons were collected somewhere somehow.
options.feedback: This option fails because praising the summary that mentions only three tons rewards the opposite partial coverage and drops the forty volunteers fact.

options.text: A concert and fireworks closed the river event.
options.feedback: This option fails because praising the summary that adds a concert and fireworks rewards invented details that appear in neither of the two reports.

questions.explanation: Judging summaries across two reports demands checking coverage, the winner mentions volunteers from report one and tons collected from report two without invention.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Announcement: Bilbao train moves to platform four. Board: Bilbao 18:30. Your friend says platform one at six. How do you correct him?
questions.context: You hear a station announcement while reading the departure board to correct a friend.

options.text: The Bilbao train now leaves at half past six from platform four.
options.feedback: Correct! Stating the Bilbao train now leaves at half past six from platform four combines the announced platform change with the board time exactly.

options.text: The Bilbao train left yesterday from platform one.
options.feedback: This option fails because stating the Bilbao train left yesterday from platform one uses a past day and old platform that match neither current source.

options.text: The Bilbao train leaves from the cafe at midnight.
options.feedback: This option fails because stating the Bilbao train leaves from the cafe at midnight invents a cafe departure and a midnight time from no source.

options.text: All trains are cancelled today.
options.feedback: This option fails because stating all trains are cancelled today contradicts both the announcement and the board, which both confirm the Bilbao departure.

questions.explanation: Correcting a friend from announcement plus board models real station multitasking, listening gives the platform change and reading confirms the new time.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Story: Lucia cycles to school every morning. Friend says every night. Which correction retells the fact correctly?
questions.context: You read a short story opening and choose the sentence that fixes a false detail for retelling.

options.text: Lucia cycles to school every morning, not every night.
options.feedback: Correct! Stating Lucia cycles to school every morning, not every night corrects only the wrong time word while keeping actor, verb and place intact.

options.text: Lucia flies to school every night.
options.feedback: This option fails because stating Lucia flies to school every night keeps the wrong night and replaces cycling with impossible flying.

options.text: Lucia never leaves her house at all.
options.feedback: This option fails because stating Lucia never leaves her house at all denies the whole true story frame instead of fixing just the time word.

options.text: Night cycles Lucia school morning.
options.feedback: This option fails because stating night cycles Lucia school morning scrambles word order into ungrammatical fragments despite containing some right words.

questions.explanation: Fixing a false statement while retelling checks careful reading plus accurate grammar, you keep the true frame and swap only the wrong time, place or actor.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Voicemail: Your visit moves to Tuesday at five. Calendar: football training Tuesday at five. What should you write?
questions.context: You listen to a voicemail about a dentist change while viewing a calendar to write back.

options.text: Thanks, Tuesday at five is noted, but it clashes with football training.
options.feedback: Correct! Confirming Tuesday at five and noting the football clash shows you heard the new time, read the calendar clash and wrote both into the reply.

options.text: Thanks, Monday at nine is perfect with no problems.
options.feedback: This option fails because confirming Monday at nine with no clash keeps an old time and misses the football clash shown on the calendar.

options.text: Thanks, Tuesday at five is fine and I will keep both appointments.
options.feedback: This option fails because confirming Tuesday at five but promising two appointments accepts the new time yet creates a double booking instead of flagging the clash.

options.text: I refuse any dentist visit ever again.
options.feedback: This option fails because refusing any dentist visit ever ignores the voicemail information and the calendar and ends communication instead of integrating sources.

questions.explanation: Voicemail into calendar into message is triple integration, you extract the new appointment fact by listening, check the clash by reading, then write politely.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: You hear: Always wear gloves. You read: Pour the liquid next. Which action integrates listening and reading safely?
questions.context: You follow spoken lab rules while reading the written steps to choose the safe action.

options.text: Wait for gloves before pouring the liquid.
options.feedback: Correct! Waiting for gloves before pouring the liquid obeys both the spoken glove warning and the written pour step in the safe combined order.

options.text: Pour the liquid now without gloves.
options.feedback: This option fails because pouring the liquid now without gloves obeys the pour step but directly disobeys the spoken glove warning about safety.

options.text: Leave the lab shouting about gloves.
options.feedback: This option fails because leaving the lab shouting about gloves abandons the written task entirely instead of sequencing gloves first and then pouring.

options.text: Taste the liquid to check its power.
options.feedback: This option fails because tasting the liquid to check its power misreads both sources dangerously and proposes an unsafe action no instruction ever allowed.

questions.explanation: Lab safety multitasking proves why integration matters, the spoken warning plus the written step together forbid the tempting shortcut that each source alone might allow.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Interviews give lively quotes. Survey: seventy percent want a garden. Which blog draft best integrates both sources?
questions.context: You compare two drafts of a class blog that should combine interview quotes and survey data.

options.text: A draft with one student quote plus seventy percent survey support.
options.feedback: Correct! Choosing the draft with one student quote plus seventy percent survey support rewards true weaving of interview voice and survey number together.

options.text: A draft with three quotes and no numbers.
options.feedback: This option fails because choosing the draft with three quotes and no numbers rewards voice only and drops the seventy percent survey evidence entirely.

options.text: A draft with only numbers and no voices.
options.feedback: This option fails because choosing the draft with only numbers and no voices rewards data only and loses the human interview perspective required.

options.text: A draft copied from last year.
options.feedback: This option fails because choosing the draft copied from last year rewards recycling that uses neither the new quotes nor the new survey data.

questions.explanation: Evaluating integrated drafts means rewarding the text that weaves a human quote together with a precise survey figure while rejecting drafts that use only one source.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Debate heard pros and cons of late buses. Vote: nine to six for late transport. Which written proposal integrates hearing, voting and writing?
questions.context: You lead a debate, a vote and a proposal that must merge arguments heard and texts read.

options.text: We propose late buses on Fridays after a nine to six vote for late transport.
options.feedback: Correct! Proposing late buses on Fridays after a nine to six vote for late transport synthesizes the heard debate, the counted vote and formal written phrasing.

options.text: We propose no buses ever for anyone.
options.feedback: This option fails because proposing no buses ever despite a nine to six vote for late transport ignores the counted majority and the debate outcome.

options.text: We propose magic carpets for all students.
options.feedback: This option fails because proposing magic carpets for all students abandons both the debate content and the vote count for a fantasy unrelated to sources.

options.text: Results now vote buses late Friday.
options.feedback: This option fails because shouting results now vote buses late Friday scrambles syntax into notes rather than a formal proposal sentence the council can adopt.

questions.explanation: Leading debate into vote into proposal is the highest multitask, you must hold opposing spoken arguments, respect the majority count and phrase the decision in formal written syntax.
questions.subject: ingles
